extracted.intended_audience: UAI 2013 paper reviewers / program committee members
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for reviewing submissions to the UAI 2013 conference: what written comments to provide, the evaluation dimensions (novelty, technical quality, impact, clarity), and how to apply the 7-point numeric score. Emphasizes constructive, specific feedback and calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address both strengths and weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Your review should address both the strengths and weaknesses of the paper - identify the areas where you believe the paper is particularly strong and particularly weak - this will be very valuable to the program chairs and the SPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit identification of where the paper excels and where it fails; be precise rather than vague. These comments are valuable for chairs/SPC to understand borderline or conflicted recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty: This is arguably the single most important criterion for selecting papers for the conference. Reviewers should reward papers that propose genuinely new ideas or novel adaptations/applications of existing methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should explicitly point out how their work is novel relative to prior work — reviewers should not be expected to infer novelty. As a reviewer, assess whether ideas are truly new, novel combinations/adaptations/extensions, or minor extensions. Novelty assessment is subjective; try to categorize degree of novelty and justify your judgment with citations to prior work when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical Quality: Are the results technically sound? Are there obvious flaws in the conceptual approach? Are claims well-supported by theoretical analysis or experimental results?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether authors ignored or appeared unaware of highly relevant prior work, whether experiments are well thought out and convincing, and whether there are obvious experiments not carried out. Evaluate replicability (will later researchers be able to replicate results?), availability of data/code, appropriateness of evaluation, sensitivity to parameter settings, and whether the authors clearly assess strengths and weaknesses of their approach. Cite specific missing references or methodological flaws if you conclude low technical quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential Impact and Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential Impact and Significance: Is this really a significant advance in the state of the art? Is this a paper that people are likely to read and cite in later years?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the paper addresses an important problem (including problems known outside UAI), whether the work is likely to have lasting impact (5–10 years), and whether researchers/practitioners might build on this work. Flag papers unlikely to have lasting impact and justify why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity of Writing: Is the paper clearly written? Does it adequately inform the reader? Is there a good use of examples and figures? Is it well organized? Are there problems with style and grammar? Are there issues with typos, formatting, references, etc.?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the full range of scores for this category to identify poorly-written papers. It is the authors' responsibility to write clearly; reviewers should not be expected to extract information from a poorly written paper. Consider whether the presentation will be understandable to future readers; if clarity is poor but the work is worthy, advise revision or provide concrete suggestions for improvement and list specific typos/format problems if relevant. Note that camera-ready time is limited, so don't assume major fixes will occur automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional Points (optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional Points (optional): An optional section on the review form to add additional comments for the authors that don’t naturally fit into any of the areas above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this section for noteworthy observations, minor suggestions, or issues not covered by the standard headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments for SPC and program chairs (optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments that are only for the SPC and program chairs (optional): If there are any comments that you would like to communicate to the SPC and program chairs, but that you do not wish to be seen by the authors, they can go in this section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place confidential or meta-level remarks (conflicts, concerns about ethical issues, submission provenance, suspicion of plagiarism, policy-related notes) here rather than in the author-facing text.

rubrics_metrics.name: General advice on review writing
rubrics_metrics.description: General Advice on Review Writing: Please be as precise as you can in your comments to the authors and avoid vague statements. Your criticism should be constructive where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If giving a low score, explain specific actions authors could take to improve (e.g., cite specific relevant prior work if you think the work is incremental). If experiments are unrealistic or insufficient, suggest improvements (more realistic datasets, larger datasets, different metrics, sensitivity analyses). Be concrete and cite examples. Avoid vague, unsupported assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeric scoring: 7-point scale
rubrics_metrics.description: For UAI 2013 we are using a 7-point scoring system. We strongly encourage you to use the full range of scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Score meanings:
7: An excellent paper, a very strong acceptance. I will fight for acceptance, this is potentially best-paper material.
6: A very good paper, should be accepted. I vote and argue for acceptance, clearly belongs in the conference.
5: A good paper overall, accept if possible. I vote for acceptance, although would not be upset if it were rejected because of the low acceptance rate.
4: Decent paper, but may be below the UAI threshold. I tend to vote for rejecting it, although would not be upset if it were accepted.
3: A weak paper, just not good enough. I vote for rejecting it, but could be persuaded otherwise.
2: A clear rejection. I vote and argue for rejection. It is clearly below the standards of the conference.
1: A strong rejection. I'm surprised it was submitted. I will actively fight for rejection.

Scoring guidance: Use the full range of scores rather than clustering in the middle; new or returning reviewers should calibrate using recent proceedings.
